sections.title: Paul and Barnabas in Iconium
observations: Paul and Barnabas arrive in Iconium, where they preach in the Jewish synagogue. Their message is met with both belief and opposition, illustrating the mixed responses to the Gospel.
The mention of signs and wonders performed by the apostles emphasizes the divine authority behind their message, validating their ministry and drawing attention to the truth of the Gospel.

sections.title: The Stoning of Paul
observations: After facing opposition, Paul and Barnabas flee to Lystra and Derbe. In Lystra, Paul heals a man who had been crippled from birth, demonstrating the power of God through faith.

The crowd's reaction to the healing shows the cultural context of the time, as they attempt to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods, revealing the challenge of communicating the Gospel in a polytheistic society.

sections.title: Return to Antioch
observations: After enduring persecution, Paul and Barnabas return to Antioch, strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to remain steadfast in their faith. This highlights the importance of community and support in the Christian journey.
The chapter concludes with a reminder of the necessity of perseverance in the face of trials, as Paul emphasizes that through many tribulations, we must enter the kingdom of God.

importantVerses.commentary: Paul and Barnabas spoke boldly for the Lord, who confirmed the message of his grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders.
Strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to remain true to the faith, saying, 'We must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God.'

questions: What does the response of the crowd in Lystra reveal about the challenges of evangelism in a pluralistic society?
How can we apply the example of Paul and Barnabas in facing opposition to our own lives today?
What does the healing of the crippled man teach us about faith and the power of God?
